T1c4a3b81c184c71b.proposition: The Privy Council must determine if a mortgagor in possession could grant a permanent lease before Section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act to bind the mortgagee.
T1c4a3b81c184c71b.standard: The question arises whether prior to the enactment of section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act in 1929 a mortgagor in possession had the power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee.
T1c4a3b81c184c71b.why_required: The core legal question for the appellate court is whether the 1925 lease was valid under the law existing at that time, specifically before the 1929 amendment.

Tc0465f0d4cbe91b2.proposition: The High Court held the 1925 permanent lease valid because it did not render the Bank's security insufficient under Section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Tc0465f0d4cbe91b2.standard: After considering all the authorities which were cited before it, it came to the conclusion that the question whether Wazir Narayan Singh had got such power or not had to be determined with reference to the provisions of section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act and the crucial test was whether the lease rendered the mortgagee's security insufficient.
Tc0465f0d4cbe91b2.why_required: The High Court applied Section 66 to assess if the lease was destructive or permanently injurious by rendering the security insufficient.

Tb6cbe9b73d77f4df.proposition: The trial court found the plaintiff subrogated to the Bank's position and the defendants bound by the mortgage decree, but the High Court negatived constructive res judicata.
Tb6cbe9b73d77f4df.standard: The trial Court hold that, the plaintiff was subrogated to the position of the Bank. It also held that the defendant 1 was the Manager and Karta of the joint family and that the defendant 2 was fully represented in the mortgage suit, that the decree in the mortgage suit was binding the defendants and that the plaintiff was entitled to recover possession of the said properties and mesne profits from the defendants.
Tb6cbe9b73d77f4df.why_required: The procedural posture regarding subrogation and res judicata was settled by the High Court, leaving only the substantive power to lease for appeal.

T972ace70bb20383b.proposition: The defendants argued the 1925 permanent lease was not binding because they were not parties to the mortgage suit and the auction sale could not end the lease.
T972ace70bb20383b.standard: He contended that the decree in the mortgage suit was not binding him as he was not a party to that suit. He further contended that the Patta could not be put an end to by the auction sale of the mortgaged property.
T972ace70bb20383b.why_required: The defendants raised specific defenses regarding privity of contract and the effect of execution sales on subsequent leases.

Tdfe00f08a81a1818.proposition: The Privy Council's final disposition on whether the mortgagor had the power to grant the lease is withheld in the provided excerpts.
Tdfe00f08a81a1818.standard: Both the Courts below found that the plaintiff was subrogated to the position of the Bank. They also found that the defendant 2 was sufficiently represented in the mortgage suit. These findings were not challenged before us and the only question which survived for our consideration was whether Wazir Narayan Singh had the power to grant a permanent lease to the defendants so as to bind the plaintiff.
Tdfe00f08a81a1818.why_required: The provided text ends before the Privy Council's judgment, leaving the ultimate resolution of the legal question open.
